questions.question: What is a lambda expression in Java and why was it introduced?
questions.title: Lambda Expressions in Java 8
questions.direct_answer: A lambda expression supplies the function method of a compatible functional interface using concise parameter-and-body syntax. Java 8 introduced it to make passing behavior less verbose, which makes APIs such as Streams practical to read. A lambda can replace some single-method anonymous-class uses, but it is not a general replacement for anonymous classes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands lambdas as a language feature and the motivation behind Java 8's functional additions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing lambda syntax without explaining functional interfaces — the type a lambda actually targets
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect lambdas to the Streams API and mention method references as the even-shorter form

sections.title: What a Lambda Expression Is
sections.content:
A **lambda expression** is a short block of code you can pass around like a value — a function with no name. You write the parameters, then `->`, then the body, and that's it.

Why it exists: before Java 8, passing behaviour meant writing an **anonymous class** — five lines of wrapper for one line of real logic. A lambda trims that wrapper away so only the logic is left.

How it works: a lambda is not a free-floating function. It targets a **functional interface** — an interface with exactly one abstract method — and becomes the body of that single method. The compiler infers the parameter types from that target, so you skip writing them.

Lambdas come in a few shapes:
- `() -> expr` — no parameters
- `s -> s.length() > 5` — one parameter, parentheses optional
- `(a, b) -> a + b` — two parameters

They are also what powers the Streams API: `filter`, `map`, and `sorted` all take lambdas.

> **The gotcha:** a lambda only works where a single-abstract-method interface is expected — point it at a regular class and it won't compile.

sections.title: Lambda at a Glance
How a Lambda Binds to a Functional Interface
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB L["Lambda
(a, b) becomes a.compareTo(b)"] --> T["Target type
a functional interface"] T --> M["Single abstract method
e.g. Comparator.compare"] L --> I["Compiler infers
the parameter types"] M --> R["Lambda becomes
that method's body"] ``` The lambda has no type of its own — it borrows the shape of whichever single-method interface is expected at that spot.

sections.title: Before lambdas vs after
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting the functional interface**: Freshers describe lambda syntax but can't name what type a lambda becomes. A lambda needs a target interface with exactly one abstract method, like `Runnable` or `Comparator` — without one, it won't compile.
- **Treating a lambda as a standalone function**: Trying to call a lambda where a plain method is expected. A lambda only fits where a functional-interface type is the expected target, not as a free function.
- **Overusing block bodies**: Wrapping a single expression in `{ return ...; }` braces. Prefer `x -> x * 2` over `x -> { return x * 2; }` when the body is one expression.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Lambda = anonymous function** — has parameters, body, return type — but no name
- **Only works with functional interfaces** — interfaces with exactly one abstract method
- **Syntax:** `(params) -> expression` or `(params) -> { statements; }`
- **Type inference:** the compiler figures out parameter types from context — you don't declare them
- **Powers the Streams API** — filter, map, sort all take lambdas as arguments

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A lambda expression is concise syntax for supplying the function method of a compatible functional interface. For example, a Comparator can be written as `(a, b) -> a.compareTo(b)` instead of an anonymous Comparator object whose only purpose is that method body. Java 8 introduced lambdas so behavior could be passed to APIs without repeated wrapper code. This is especially useful in Stream operations: `filter` accepts a Predicate and `map` accepts a Function, and a lambda can provide either implementation. The target functional-interface type is essential because it tells the compiler the parameter and return types. Lambdas replace suitable single-method anonymous-class cases, but an anonymous class remains different: it creates its own class scope, has its own `this`, and can declare fields and extra methods.

questions.question: What is 'effectively final' and why do lambdas require it?
questions.title: Effectively Final Variables in Lambdas
questions.direct_answer: 'Effectively final' means a local variable or parameter is never reassigned after its initial assignment. A lambda may capture it without an explicit `final` keyword, but the lambda captures the value of that local variable rather than sharing a mutable local-variable slot.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of variable capture and why the JVM enforces the effectively-final rule
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying the variable must be declared final — effectively final means the compiler infers it, no keyword needed
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that a lambda captures the local variable's value, while the object referenced by that value may still be mutable; thread safety is a separate issue

sections.title: What 'Effectively Final' Means
sections.content:
**Effectively final** means a local variable or parameter is not reassigned after its initial assignment. Java can therefore let a lambda capture it without requiring the `final` keyword.

The important model is capture by value. If `name` refers to a String, the lambda receives that reference value; it does not share a local-variable slot that surrounding code can later point somewhere else. This rule also keeps lambda capture consistent with local and anonymous classes. It should not be explained as a promise about one JVM memory location or as automatic thread safety.

How the compiler decides:
- Assign once and never reassign → effectively final → capture compiles.
- Reassign on any reachable path → not effectively final → capture does not compile.

That is why `count++` or `name = "new"` breaks capture. The rule is about the variable, not the referenced object: a captured `List` reference can remain fixed while the list's contents change. Such mutation may still need synchronization when threads share the object.

sections.title: Capture Rules at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Effectively final|~initialised once|never reassigned|no `final` keyword needed|compiler checks it
blue|Capture model|~captures the local value|does not share a mutable local slot|referenced object may still change|thread safety is separate
emerald|What breaks it|~count++|name = "new"|reassignment after init|then capture won't compile

sections.title: When Capture Compiles and When It Breaks
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A["Local variable
assigned a value"] --> B{"Reassigned
later?"} B -- No --> C["Effectively final
lambda captures a copy"] B -- Yes --> D["Not effectively final
compile error"] C --> E["Lambda can run later
the value stays stable"] ``` The single question the compiler asks is whether the variable is ever reassigned — everything else follows from that.

sections.title: Effectively final — what works and what doesn't
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking you must write `final`**: Believing the variable needs the `final` keyword. Effectively final means the compiler infers it — no keyword is needed as long as you never reassign.
- **Reassigning a captured variable**: Updating a counter or accumulator like `total += x` in the surrounding method, then wondering why the lambda no longer compiles.
- **Reaching for the array hack**: Using a single-element array `int[] c = {0}` to fake a mutable counter inside a lambda. It compiles, but it's a code smell and is unsafe across threads.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Effectively final** — a local variable or parameter is never reassigned after its initial assignment; no `final` keyword is required
- **Capture by value** — the lambda captures the local value, not a mutable local-variable slot
- **What breaks it** — reassignment such as `count++` or `name = ...`
- **Reassignment, not mutation** — a captured `List` reference can stay fixed while its contents change
- **Thread safety is separate** — being effectively final does not make the referenced object immutable or safe to share

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
When a lambda captures a local variable or parameter, that variable must be final or effectively final. Effectively final simply means it is not reassigned after its initial assignment; the `final` keyword is optional.

The lambda captures the local variable's value rather than sharing a local slot that surrounding code can later reassign. If the value is an object reference, both the lambda and surrounding code can still see the same object, so changing that object's contents is possible and may require normal thread-safety care.

For example, a lambda can read a `List` stored in an effectively-final variable and even add to that list, but it cannot assign a different list to the local variable. Writing `count++` also counts as reassignment and prevents `count` from being captured. Fields follow different rules and may be read or written from the lambda, subject to ordinary access and concurrency rules.

questions.question: Can a lambda expression access instance variables and static variables?
questions.title: Variable Access Inside Lambdas
questions.direct_answer: Yes. A lambda can read and write accessible instance and static fields; the effectively-final capture rule applies to local variables and parameters, not fields. Inside an instance context, `this` has the same meaning as in the enclosing code. Field access is still subject to normal access-control and thread-safety rules.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of which variable kinds a lambda can mutate and how 'this' behaves inside a lambda
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming instance fields have the same effectively-final restriction as local variables
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Contrast lexical `this` in a lambda with the anonymous-class instance's own `this`, and separate compile-time access from thread safety

sections.title: Lambda Variable Access
sections.content:
Inside a lambda, accessible instance and static fields can be read or assigned. The final/effectively-final rule is specifically about captured local variables and parameters.

The difference is a language rule about capture, not a simple stack-versus-heap rule. A lambda captures the value of a local variable, so Java does not allow that local to be reassigned. A field is reached through an object or class and is not a captured local-variable slot, so normal field assignment rules apply.

A quick summary:
- Captured local variable or parameter → must be final or effectively final.
- Accessible instance field → can be read or written through the enclosing instance.
- Accessible static field → can be read or written through the class.

In an instance context, `this` inside a lambda means the same enclosing instance as it does outside the lambda. An anonymous class is different: its body has its own `this`. None of these rules make shared mutation thread-safe; a lambda running concurrently still needs normal synchronization or atomic state.

sections.title: Access by Variable Kind
sections.content:
amber|Captured local|~must be final or effectively final|lambda captures its value|reference may point to mutable data|thread safety is separate
blue|Instance + static fields|~normal read and write rules|not subject to local capture restriction|access control still applies|shared writes may race
emerald|`this` keyword|~same meaning as enclosing context|instance lambda uses enclosing object|anonymous class has its own `this`|static context has no `this`

sections.title: What a Lambda Can Do per Variable Kind
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A["Name used
inside a lambda"] --> B{"Which kind?"} B -- Local or parameter --> C["May be captured only when
final or effectively final"] B -- Instance field --> D["Normal field access
through enclosing instance"] B -- Static field --> E["Normal field access
through the class"] C --> F["Captured value may still
refer to mutable data"] ``` This is a capture rule for locals, not a promise that field writes or referenced objects are thread-safe.

sections.title: Lambda variable access — all three types
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Applying the local-capture rule to fields**: fields are accessed through an object or class, so they do not have to be effectively final.
- **Misreading `this`**: in an instance context, `this` inside a lambda is the enclosing instance; an anonymous class body has its own `this`. A static context has no `this` to capture.
- **Confusing legal access with safe access**: writing a shared field is allowed by the compiler but can still create a data race.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Captured locals and parameters** — must be final or effectively final
- **Instance fields** — normal accessible field reads and writes are allowed
- **Static fields** — normal accessible class-field reads and writes are allowed
- **`this` in an instance lambda** — has the same meaning as in the enclosing context
- **Concurrency** — permitted field or object mutation is not automatically thread-safe

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A lambda can read and write accessible instance and static fields. The final or effectively-final rule applies to captured local variables and parameters, not to fields.

For example, a lambda may read a local request ID only if that local is not reassigned. It may also increment an instance counter or a static counter because those are field accesses. That is legal Java, but if several threads run the lambda, the counter still needs normal synchronization or an atomic type.

In an instance context, `this` inside the lambda has the same meaning as in the surrounding method: it refers to the enclosing object. An anonymous class body differs because it introduces its own `this`. In a static context there is no enclosing `this` at all.
